title: Who commands, who answers? The legal accountability of foreign police in the Pacific
author: Nasser Zakr

The legal accountability of foreign police in the PacificExperience in Papua New Guinea and Solomon Islands show that one Pacific policing body won’t by itself resolve who is legally responsible when officers act abroad.Nasser Zakr 20 November 20264 min read|Who commands, who answers? The legal accountability of foreign police in the PacificWho commands, who answers? The legal accountability of foreign police in the PacificSending police abroad to serve in situations of strife raises tricky practical considerations – the importance of defining police powers, command relationships and institutional responsibilities. The Pacific faces such a question now: who is legally responsible when police officers exercise public authority beyond their own national jurisdiction?The endorsement of the Constitution of the Pacific Community of Policing (PACPOL) on 14 October 2026 (Opens in new window) brings the Pacific Islands Chiefs of Police (PICP) and the Pacific Policing Initiative (PPI) under a single, Pacific-led framework. But institutional unity does not, by itself, settle questions of command, jurisdiction or accountability.The Pacific already has a relevant example, and it has already been activated. The 2017 Agreement between Australia and Solomon Islands concerning the deployment of police, armed forces and other personnel (Opens in new window), signed on 14 August 2017 and in force since 13 June 2018, was invoked in November 2021, when Solomon Islands requested assistance following unrest in Honiara.The agreement distributes authority among different institutions.Under Article 4, visiting Australian police remain under national command, while the senior Australian police officer commands the Assisting Police Force. Members of the Assisting Police Force may exercise the powers and privileges of members of the Royal Solomon Islands Police Force, but are not subject to local disciplinary rules or the jurisdiction of Solomon Islands disciplinary authorities, courts or tribunals.PACPOL unifies Pacific policing's leadership, but each deployment still turns on a separate agreement over command and redress.Article 6 grants members of a Visiting Contingent immunity from arrest, detention and legal proceedings in Solomon Islands for acts performed in the course of, or incidental to, official duties. This covers criminal, civil, disciplinary, administrative and customary law proceedings. Australia or a contributing third state may waive the immunity of its own personnel, and the agreement regulates the exercise of criminal and disciplinary jurisdiction by those states.Article 22 provides that third-party claims arising from official acts and resulting in property damage, injury or death are handled under Solomon Islands law, including evidence-gathering and the allocation of compensation costs.The lesson is not that such arrangements are inappropriate. It is that the authority to exercise police powers, operational command, disciplinary control, criminal jurisdiction and responsibility for compensation are distinct matters. Their relationship should be settled before personnel are deployed.Papua New Guinea’s experience shows why these allocations need constitutional scrutiny. In May 2005, its Supreme Court considered the Enhanced Cooperation between Papua New Guinea and Australia Act 2004 in Special Reference by the Morobe Provincial Executive (SC785) (Opens in new window). The Court unanimously (Opens in new window) found the immunity provisions unconstitutional, including the exclusion of the civil jurisdiction of Papua New Guinea’s courts over acts done in the course of official duties. It led to the withdrawal of the Australian police contingent (Opens in new window).The decision did not reject international police assistance. It showed that arrangements allowing foreign personnel to exercise public authority must comply with the host state’s constitution. Solomon Islands’ constitutional framework is different, but Article 6 raises a comparable question: how can immunity serve legitimate operational purposes while still leaving an effective avenue for valid claims?These examples matter as PACPOL moves from design to implementation. A regional policing body is not a supranational police authority. PACPOL will be led by a single Chiefs Leadership Board (Opens in new window) providing strategic oversight, while the powers conferred on foreign personnel will continue to depend on specific deployment agreements.Three principles deserve attention.First, the legal basis and limits of cross-border deployments should be clearly established. The powers of visiting personnel and their relationship with the host country’s police and judicial institutions need to be defined in advance.Second, operational command and legal accountability should be addressed separately. Agreements should identify the authorities responsible for investigating alleged misconduct, exercising criminal and disciplinary jurisdiction, and obtaining and sharing evidence.Third, individuals affected by the conduct of deployed personnel should have effective procedures for seeking redress. Immunities may serve legitimate operational purposes, but they should not leave valid claims without a legal avenue.PACPOL is well placed to turn these principles into practice. It could develop model provisions for deployment agreements covering command, jurisdiction, evidence-sharing and claims. It could also encourage member states to establish a regional channel through which people affected by the conduct of deployed personnel can have complaints referred to the appropriate national authorities. This would respect national sovereignty while strengthening mutual confidence.Cross-border policing needs more than agreement on who may exercise police powers. It requires clarity about who is legally responsible for their exercise. That clarity is not an obstacle to cooperation; it is one of the conditions of its legitimacy.About the authorNasser Zakr Nasser Zakr is a lawyer specialising in international law and human rights.
